draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was he directly involved in the car accident, rather than merely witnessing it?"}
review: There is no prior history, so this hasn’t been asked or rejected. The proposed question is plausible, but “directly involved” is ambiguous: it could mean injured, a participant, or simply present nearby. A clearer discriminating question is: “Did his stopping to tie his shoelace play a causal role in the accident?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did his stopping to tie his shoelace play a causal role in the accident?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was he himself struck or otherwise physically involved in the car accident?"}
review: The history establishes only that stopping to tie his shoelace played a causal role; it doesn’t establish that he was struck or physically involved. Your question is a reasonable probe, but “otherwise physically involved” is broad. A more discriminating version: “Did his body physically interact with a vehicle as part of the causal chain?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did his body physically interact with a vehicle as part of the causal chain?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did a driver cause the accident while reacting to seeing him squat down?"}
review: The proposed question assumes both that a driver was the cause and that the driver saw him squat; neither is established. The history only confirms that stopping played some causal role and rules out his body physically interacting with a vehicle. Ask a broader, discriminating question instead: “Did his stopping cause the accident by changing another road user’s movement or attention?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did his stopping cause another road user to change their actions?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the accident a real collision involving full-sized road vehicles?"}
review: The proposed question adds unsupported assumptions: the story does not establish that this was a real-world collision or that full-sized vehicles were involved. The “no” to physical interaction does not rule out a vehicle collision; it only rules out the stated bodily interaction. The history also says the stop mattered causally, but not how, and that it did not change another road user’s actions. A more discriminating question: “Did stopping change his own position or timing in a way that affected the accident?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did stopping to tie his shoelace change his position or timing in a way that affected the accident?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did tying his shoelace prevent him from being injured or killed in the car accident?"}
review: The proposed question assumes he was in danger of being injured or killed; nothing in the history establishes that. The feedback only says his stop affected the accident through his position or timing, while ruling out physical interaction with a vehicle and changing another road user’s actions. No earlier question repeats this injury hypothesis. A broader, discriminating question is: “Would the accident still have happened if he had not stopped to tie his shoelace?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Would the accident still have happened if he had not stopped to tie his shoelace?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was he himself involved in the car accident, either as a driver or a passenger?"}
review: The proposal is unasked, but “driver or passenger” is too narrow: it excludes other ways he might be directly involved and assumes his role is vehicle-related. The history only establishes that his stopping affected the accident through position or timing; it does not establish how. Ask: “Was he one of the people directly involved in the accident?” This tests personal involvement without presuming a specific role or mechanism.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was he one of the people directly involved in the accident?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did the accident involve a collision between two vehicles?"}
review: The proposal assumes a two-vehicle collision, which no feedback supports. The history says his stop causally changed timing or position, but he wasn’t directly involved, his body didn’t interact with a vehicle, and he didn’t make another road user change their actions. A more discriminating, mechanism-neutral question: “Did his stop affect whether someone else was at the accident location when it happened?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did his stop affect whether someone else was at the accident location when it happened?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the accident a traffic accident involving motor vehicles?"}
review: The proposed question is low-value: the opening already calls it a “car accident,” and whether motor vehicles were involved does little to explain the established causal role. The history also rules out direct physical contact, changing another road user’s actions, his direct involvement, and affecting whether someone else was at the scene. Don’t infer a specific mechanism from the mixed clues. A more discriminating question is: “Did his stop change the timing of the accident itself, rather than only his own timing or position?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did his stop change the timing of the accident itself, rather than only his own timing or position?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the accident a collision between two or more vehicles?"}
review: The proposed question is possible, but it doesn’t address the key unresolved point: how his stop affected the accident despite no direct involvement, vehicle contact, changed actions by another road user, or change to the accident’s timing. It also assumes a vehicle collision that the opening doesn’t establish. A more discriminating question: “Did stopping cause a physical condition at the scene that contributed to the accident?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did stopping to tie his shoelace cause a physical condition at the scene that contributed to the accident?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did he leave or drop an object or substance at the scene while tying his shoelace, and did that contribute to the accident?"}
review: The proposal is plausible but unsupported: the history confirms a scene condition contributed to the accident, not that he left or dropped an object or substance. It also bundles two claims, making a “yes” ambiguous. A cleaner discriminating question is: “Was the relevant physical condition a hazard on the roadway?” This avoids guessing its source. The history already rules out his direct involvement, physical contact with a vehicle, changing another road user’s actions, changing the accident’s timing, and affecting who was at the location—don’t revisit those.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the physical condition that contributed to the accident a hazard on the roadway?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did he leave or place an object at the scene while stopping to tie his shoelace, and did that object contribute to the accident?"}
review: The object-left-behind idea is possible, but nothing in the history establishes an object; the “physical condition” could have another cause. The proposal also bundles leaving/placing an object with its contribution to the accident. This has not already been asked or rejected, but the prior “not a roadway hazard” answer rules out only that category. Ask a broader discriminator: “Did he cause a physical change to the surroundings while tying his shoe that contributed to the accident?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did he cause a physical change to the surroundings while tying his shoe that contributed to the accident?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"While tying his shoelace, did he accidentally move, drop, or damage an object that later contributed to the accident?"}
review: The proposal is plausible but too specific: the history supports that he caused some physical change to the surroundings, not that an object was moved, dropped, or damaged. Those are untested mechanisms, and the earlier “no” answers only rule out bodily contact with a vehicle, changed actions by another road user, and a roadway hazard. Ask a broader discriminator instead: “Did he alter an object that was already there, rather than leave or introduce something?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did he alter an object that was already there, rather than leave or introduce something?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did he leave behind an object he had brought from the supermarket, and did that object contribute to the accident?"}
review: The proposed question is too specific: nothing in the feedback establishes that he had an item from the supermarket, left it behind, or that it caused the accident. The earlier “alter an object already there, rather than leave or introduce something?” got “no,” but that does not prove he left an object—the relevant change could be something else. A better discriminator is: “Was the physical change something he left behind at the scene?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the physical change something he left behind at the scene?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the thing he left behind an item he had bought at the supermarket?"}
review: The supermarket-item question is an unsupported narrowing: nothing so far says the thing was bought there or even was an item. The history already rules out a roadway hazard and altering an object that was already there; it establishes only that he caused a physical change and left something behind. A more discriminating next question would be: “Was what he left behind a discrete object, rather than a mark or other physical trace?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was what he left behind a discrete object, rather than a mark or other physical trace?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the object he left behind something he had bought at the supermarket?"}
review: The proposed question assumes the object was a supermarket purchase; nothing in the feedback establishes its source. The history also contains no repeated question or rejected hypothesis to avoid. A broader, more useful discriminator is: “Was the object already in his possession when he stopped, rather than something he picked up or created at the spot?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the object already in his possession before he stopped to tie his shoe?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the object he left behind something he had bought at the supermarket?"}
review: The proposed question is new, but “bought at the supermarket” is a narrow guess with no support in the history. We know the object was already in his possession and was left behind; we do not know what it was or how it contributed. Earlier answers rule out a roadway hazard and say his stop did not change another road user’s actions, but they do not establish the object’s role. A more discriminating question: “Did the object contribute directly by causing a physical event, rather than indirectly by prompting someone to act?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the object contribute directly by causing a physical event, rather than indirectly by prompting someone to act?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the object he left behind something he had just bought at the supermarket?"}
review: The supermarket-purchase question is plausible, but the setting doesn’t establish that the object was something he bought; it could have been another possession. The history already establishes that he left a discrete object he possessed before stopping, and that it contributed through a direct physical event—not through a roadway hazard or another person’s reaction. A broader, more discriminating question would be: “Was the object something he was carrying at the time?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the object something he was carrying at the time?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did the object he left behind physically strike or make contact with a vehicle involved in the accident?"}
review: The proposed question is not already rejected: the earlier “no” was about his body contacting a vehicle, not the object he left behind. But the history does not establish that the object struck a vehicle; it could have caused a physical event another way. A broader, still discriminating question: “Did the object physically contact anything involved in the accident?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the object physically contact anything involved in the accident?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the object he left behind something he had bought at the supermarket?"}
review: The proposed question is possible, but nothing in the history establishes that the object was bought at the supermarket; it only establishes that he already possessed and carried it. Whether it was a purchase may not clarify how it contributed. A more discriminating next question: “Did the object physically contact one of the vehicles involved in the accident?” This tests a specific, still-open part of the causal chain without assuming what the object was.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the object physically contact one of the vehicles involved in the accident?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the object something he had just bought at the supermarket?"}
review: The proposed supermarket-purchase question is unsupported: the history only establishes that he already possessed the object before stopping, and its origin has not been established. It also doesn’t directly distinguish how the object contributed after being left behind and contacting a vehicle. A more useful question is: “Did he intentionally put the object down while tying his shoe, rather than accidentally drop it?” This tests a causal detail without assuming what the object was or how it contacted the vehicle.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did he intentionally put the object down while tying his shoe, rather than accidentally drop it?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"After he set the object down, did it move and strike a vehicle?"}
review: The proposed question assumes the object moved after being set down and that it struck the vehicle. The history establishes only that he deliberately put down an object he was carrying, and that it physically contacted a vehicle and directly contributed to the accident; it does not establish which moved or the direction of contact. This is not a repeated question, but it narrows the mechanism without support. Better discriminator: “Did a vehicle strike the object, rather than the object striking the vehicle?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did a vehicle strike the object, rather than the object striking the vehicle?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"After he put the object down, did it move and then strike a vehicle?"}
review: The proposed question adds an unestablished sequence: the history confirms the object contacted a vehicle, but the “no” to “Did a vehicle strike the object, rather than the object striking the vehicle?” does not prove the object moved and struck it. It also revisits contact direction without resolving how the object got there. Ask instead: “Did the object move after he put it down and before it contacted the vehicle?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the object move after he put it down and before it contacted the vehicle?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the object a shopping bag or something he bought at the supermarket?"}
review: The shopping connection is plausible from the opening, but nothing in the history establishes that the object was a bag or something he bought; it could simply have been another item he was carrying. The proposed question also bundles two possibilities. No shopping-bag hypothesis has already been rejected. A cleaner discriminator is: “Was the object something he had just bought at the supermarket?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the object something he had just bought at the supermarket?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did he put the object on or against a vehicle while tying his shoe?"}
review: The proposed question is plausible, but the history doesn’t establish that he put the object on or against a vehicle. We know he set down an object he was carrying, it stayed still, and it later contacted a vehicle; the “vehicle struck it” question received “no,” which doesn’t resolve the exact contact sequence. A more discriminating question is: **“Was the object already touching a vehicle when he put it down?”**
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the object already touching a vehicle when he put it down?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the vehicle he touched with the object parked or stationary when he put the object down?"}
review: The proposed question is reasonable but may not distinguish the key possibilities: the object was already touching a vehicle when he put it down, and it did not move before contact. Ask instead: “After he put the object down, did the vehicle move in a way that contributed to the accident?” This tests what happened next without assuming the vehicle was parked or specifying a mechanism. The history already rules out the vehicle striking the object, so avoid building that into a theory.
action: {"type":"question","text":"After he put the object down, did the vehicle move in a way that contributed to the accident?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did the object cause the accident by obstructing a driver's view?"}
review: The view-obstruction hypothesis is unsupported: the history establishes that the stationary object was already touching a vehicle when he placed it down, and that the vehicle later moved in a way that contributed to the accident. It does not establish that anyone’s view was blocked. Ask: “Did the object physically interfere with the vehicle’s movement or operation?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the object physically interfere with the vehicle’s movement?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the vehicle stationary when he put the object down against it?"}
review: The proposal targets an unanswered detail, but “put the object down against it” is stronger than the history supports: we only know the object was already touching a vehicle when he put it down. Repair the question to: “Was the vehicle stationary when he put the object down?” This is distinct from the already-answered questions about whether the object moved afterward and whether the vehicle later moved; neither establishes its state at placement.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the vehicle stationary when he put the object down?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did the object obstruct the driver's view when the vehicle moved?"}
review: The proposed question assumes there was a driver whose view the object could obstruct; the history doesn’t establish that. Also, “Did the object physically interfere with the vehicle’s movement?” was already answered no, so don’t simply repackage that as a visibility theory. A broader discriminating question: “Did the object contribute to the accident through its effect on a person in or near the vehicle?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the object contribute to the accident through its effect on a person in or near the vehicle?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did the object contribute by startling or distracting someone in the vehicle?"}
review: The proposed question is too specific: nothing establishes that anyone was startled or distracted, and the history says the object caused a physical event rather than merely prompting someone to act. Ask a broader discriminator instead: “Did the object cause a bodily reaction or movement in someone in or near the vehicle?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the object cause a bodily reaction or movement in someone in or near the vehicle?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the vehicle unoccupied when he placed the object against it?"}
review: The question is plausible and not repeated or already rejected. But it focuses on occupancy when he placed the object, while the feedback only establishes that the object later affected someone in or near the vehicle. That person could have approached or entered afterward. A better discriminator is: “When the object affected the person, were they inside the vehicle?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"When the object affected the person, were they inside the vehicle?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did the object affect the person inside the vehicle through a sensory stimulus, such as sight, sound, or smell?"}
review: This is a useful next question, not a conclusion: the history supports that the object affected someone inside the vehicle, but does not establish a sensory mechanism. It also rules out a bodily reaction or movement, so avoid presuming a startle or evasive action. The sensory-stimulus question is not a repeat of the rejected question about prompting another person to act; it distinguishes perception from other possible effects. I’d ask it as proposed, without guessing which sense or what the person perceived.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the object affect the person inside the vehicle through a sensory stimulus, such as sight, sound, or smell?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the sensory stimulus visual?"}
review: The proposed question is a useful, non-repeated discriminator: the history establishes that the object affected someone inside the vehicle through a sensory stimulus, but does not establish which sense. Asking whether it was visual does not assume that it was.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the sensory stimulus visual?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did he place the object on the outside of the vehicle, such as on its hood or roof?"}
review: The proposed question is possible, but “on the outside” (and the hood/roof examples) adds a location detail the history doesn’t establish. We know the object was touching a stationary vehicle when he put it down, and its visual stimulus affected someone inside; we don’t know where it was placed or who saw it. A more discriminating next question is: “Was the person inside the vehicle who saw the object the driver?” The history has not already asked or rejected that.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the person inside the vehicle who saw the object the driver?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did the passenger communicate what they saw to the driver, and did that communication contribute to the accident?"}
review: The proposal is plausible, but the history establishes only that someone other than the driver inside the vehicle saw the object. It does not establish that this person was a passenger, communicated what they saw, or that any communication contributed to the accident. The question also bundles communication with causation. Earlier answers say the object contributed directly through a physical event, not indirectly by prompting someone to act, so a communication-based explanation may conflict with that feedback. Ask one discriminating question first: “Did the person inside the vehicle who saw the object tell the driver about it before the accident?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the person inside the vehicle who saw the object tell the driver about it before the accident?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the object placed on the outside of the vehicle, where the passenger could see it through a window?"}
review: The proposed question bundles several unsupported details: that the object was outside the vehicle, visible through a window, and visible to the passenger from that position. The history establishes only that the object touched a vehicle and that a passenger saw it; it also says the passenger did not tell the driver, and the object caused no bodily reaction or movement. Ask instead: “Did the passenger’s seeing the object contribute to the accident through an effect on the driver?” This tests a possible link without presuming where the object was or how it was seen.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the passenger’s seeing the object contribute to the accident through an effect on the driver?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the passenger who saw the object injured in the accident?"}
review: The injury question is possible but weakly discriminating: whether the passenger was injured may be an outcome, not the mechanism by which seeing the object contributed. The history already rules out the passenger telling the driver, affecting the driver, and a bodily reaction or movement. It does not establish that the passenger was injured or that injury explains the accident. A better next question: “Did the passenger’s seeing the object contribute through an effect on someone other than the driver?” This tests a remaining broad causal route without guessing a specific mechanism.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the passenger’s seeing the object contribute through an effect on someone other than the driver?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did the accident occur because the driver lost control of the vehicle?"}
review: The “lost control” mechanism is unsupported: the history establishes that the vehicle moved and the object affected an occupant visually, but does not establish that the driver lost control. The passenger’s seeing the object was explicitly said not to affect the driver or anyone else, so don’t treat that as a confirmed explanation. A useful next question is: “Did the driver see the object before the accident?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the driver see the object before the accident?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the vehicle the object was already touching one of the vehicles involved in the accident?"}
review: The proposed question is distinct, but the history already strongly links the stationary vehicle to the accident: it moved in a contributing way, and the object contacted an accident vehicle. So confirming that the vehicle it touched at placement was involved may add little. More importantly, the causal route remains unclear: the passenger saw the object, but their seeing did not affect the driver or anyone else, and no bodily reaction or movement was reported. A broader discriminating question: “Did the passenger’s own actions or decisions after seeing the object contribute to the accident?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the passenger take an action or make a decision after seeing the object that contributed to the accident?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did the passenger’s sight of the object cause an emotional or psychological response that contributed to the accident?"}
review: The proposed question is too narrow and runs into prior answers: the passenger’s seeing the object was already said not to contribute through an effect on the driver or anyone else, and not to lead to an action or decision that contributed. An emotional response is another specific human-effect mechanism, not a conclusion supported by the history. Ask instead: “Did the passenger’s seeing the object contribute to the accident through a mechanism other than affecting another person?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the passenger’s seeing the object contribute to the accident through a mechanism other than affecting another person?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the person inside the vehicle who saw the object a child?"}
review: The child question is unsupported: nothing in the history points to the occupant’s age. More importantly, the passenger’s seeing the object has already been ruled out as contributing through the driver, anyone else, or another mechanism, so this likely revisits a rejected path. A more discriminating question is: “Did the object contribute by obstructing someone’s view of something relevant to the accident, rather than by prompting anyone to act?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the object contribute by obstructing someone’s view of something relevant to the accident, rather than by prompting anyone to act?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did the object obstruct the driver’s view of something relevant to the accident?"}
review: The proposed question is a useful discriminator, but the driver is not established as the person whose view was obstructed. The fact that the driver did not see the object does not show that it blocked the driver’s view. Ask this to distinguish who was affected: “Was the obstructed view the driver’s?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the obstructed view the driver’s?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did he place the object against the vehicle’s windshield, where it obstructed the driver’s view?"}
review: The history strongly supports that the object was left touching a stationary vehicle and obstructed the driver’s view, but it does not establish that it was on the windshield. The proposed question bundles that unsupported location with an already-confirmed effect. No identical windshield question appears in the history. A less leading discriminator: “Was the object on a transparent surface of the vehicle, such as a window or windshield?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the object on a transparent surface of the vehicle, such as a window or windshield?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the object placed on the vehicle’s hood?"}
review: The hood is an unsupported guess: the history establishes that the object was deliberately placed touching a stationary vehicle, later obstructed the driver’s view, and was not on a transparent surface—but it does not establish which part of the vehicle it was on. The hood has not been asked about before, but the broader placement question is more informative: **“Was the object on the vehicle’s exterior?”** A yes would support the proposed direction without prematurely assuming the hood; a no would redirect the search. The passenger-related routes and roadway-hazard hypothesis have already been rejected, so avoid reopening them.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the object on the vehicle’s exterior?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did he place the object on the vehicle’s hood (bonnet)?"}
review: The hood is plausible but unsupported: the history establishes only that the object was placed on the vehicle’s exterior and obstructed the driver’s view; it does not establish which exterior surface. No earlier question specifically tests the hood. Ask a broader discriminator: “Was the object on the vehicle’s front exterior, where it blocked the driver’s view of the road ahead?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the object on the vehicle’s front exterior, where it blocked the driver’s view of the road ahead?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the object a bag of groceries that he placed on the car’s hood?"}
review: The proposed question is too specific: the history establishes that the object was bought at the supermarket and placed on the stationary vehicle’s front exterior, but not that it was a grocery bag or on the hood. Neither detail has been tested; don’t treat them as established. The broader obstruction mechanism has already been confirmed, so avoid repeating it. A more discriminating next question is: “Did the driver fail to see the other vehicle or road hazard involved because the object blocked their view?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the object block the driver’s view of another vehicle involved in the accident?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did the object block the driver’s view of a pedestrian involved in the accident?"}
review: The pedestrian-specific question is plausible but unsupported: nothing in the history establishes that the obstructed thing was a pedestrian. The last answer was “irrelevant,” not “no,” so it does not rule out another vehicle either. A better discriminator is: “Did the object block the driver’s view of a person or road user?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the object block the driver’s view of a person or road user involved in the accident?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the object a shopping bag that he placed on the car’s hood?"}
review: The history supports that it was a newly purchased object he deliberately set down while touching a stationary vehicle’s front exterior, where it blocked the driver’s view. It does not establish that the object was a shopping bag or that the surface was the hood. The proposed question bundles those two unknowns, so a “no” would not tell you which is wrong. Ask first: “Was the object a bag?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the object a bag?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the object a large item, such as a box or package, that obstructed the driver’s view from the front of the vehicle?"}
review: The proposal is too leading: the history establishes that the object blocked the driver’s view, but not that it was large, a box, or a package. “Bag” has already been rejected, so don’t circle back to that category. The two “which thing did it block?” questions were marked irrelevant; that feedback doesn’t establish a particular target or mechanism. Better ask a neutral category question, such as: “Was the object a piece of produce?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the object a piece of produce?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did the accident happen because the driver could not see a stationary obstacle in the road ahead?"}
review:
Reject the proposed wording: the history establishes that the object blocked the driver’s forward view, but not that the driver missed a *stationary obstacle* or that the accident happened by hitting one. The questions about whether the blocked view concerned another vehicle or a person were both marked irrelevant, so don’t presume either target. The passenger-related routes (telling the driver, affecting someone, or taking action) were already rejected; don’t revisit them.

A less assumptive, useful question: **“Did the blocked view cause the driver to collide with something?”**
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the blocked view cause the driver to collide with something?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the object a large item in a box or other packaging?"}
review: The boxed-item guess is plausible, but neither “large” nor “in a box” is supported by the history. We already know it was a newly bought item, left on the vehicle’s front exterior, and blocked the driver’s forward view; bags and produce have been ruled out. Ask a broader, discriminating question instead: “Was the item’s size or shape what obstructed the driver’s view?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the item’s size or shape what obstructed the driver’s view?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did the object obstruct the driver’s view by reflecting light or creating glare?"}
review: The glare/reflection idea is possible but unsupported: nothing in the history establishes the object’s material or that it reflected light. The history already says it obstructed the driver’s view of the road ahead and that size or shape was not the cause; it also rules out the passenger, driver seeing the object, and prompting anyone to act as the mechanism. A more discriminating question would be: “Was the driver’s view blocked because the object physically lay in the driver’s line of sight, rather than through an optical effect such as glare?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the driver’s view blocked because the object physically lay in the driver’s line of sight, rather than through an optical effect such as glare?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the item a rigid container, such as a box, carton, or can?"}
review: The rigid-container question is an unsupported narrowing: nothing in the history points to a box, carton, or can, and the item is already known not to be a bag or produce. A more discriminating question would test the unresolved physical property: “Was the item opaque, so it blocked the driver’s view by obscuring what was behind it?” This builds on the established direct obstruction without assuming a specific kind of supermarket item.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the item opaque, blocking the driver’s view by obscuring what was behind it?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the object a packaged food item?"}
review: The proposed question is not repeated, but “packaged food item” is an unsupported narrowing: the history establishes that it was a purchased, carried object, not that it was food or packaged. A more discriminating, less assumptive question would be: “Was the object packaging or a container for something he bought, rather than the purchased item itself?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the object packaging or a container for something he bought, rather than the purchased item itself?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the object a piece of clothing or fabric?"}

Later, the driver operated the wipers, whose movement transferred or smeared the egg into the driver’s line of sight, obstructing the view and contributing to a collision. The man was not directly involved in the accident, but his stop led him to leave the egg on the car, and without that, the accident would not have happened."}

review: The proposed chain is largely supported, but “where the wipers would carry it” implies the man knew or intended that outcome; the history only establishes that he deliberately set down the egg and the wipers later moved its smear into the driver’s sightline. “On his way home” is also not established. The two near-identical final explanations already received mixed feedback, so repeating them with the same assumptions may not resolve the problem. On this mandatory final, keep to the established facts and avoid guessing the exact wiper component or what the driver collided with: Returning from the supermarket, the man stopped to tie his shoelace and deliberately set down an egg he had just bought against a component of a stationary vehicle’s windshield-wiper mechanism. The egg broke or smeared there. Later, the driver operated the wipers, and their movement transferred or spread the egg into the driver’s line of sight, obstructing the view and contributing to a collision. The man was not directly involved; without his stop and the egg left on the vehicle, the accident would not have happened.
